memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: "The Lord will bring a nation against you from far away, from the ends of the earth, like an eagle swooping down, a nation whose language you will not understand... They will lay siege to all the cities throughout your land until the high fortified walls in which you trust fall down. Because of the suffering your enemy will inflict on you during the siege, you will eat the fruit of the womb, the flesh of the sons and daughters the Lord your God has given you." — Deut 28:49-53 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
This is among the most horrifying passages in all of Scripture — the description of a siege so desperate that people would turn to the unthinkable to survive. It is deliberately shocking. God does not sanitise the horror of what unrestrained sin and judgment lead to. He shows the full, dreadful end of the road so that His people might turn back before reaching it.

We should not read this quickly or comfortably. It is meant to disturb us. And it reminds us that sin is not a small thing. Left unchecked, rebellion against God unravels everything, even the most basic bonds of human love and family. The horror of the siege is the horror of a world where God's restraining mercy is fully withdrawn.

Passages like this are hard for tender hearts, so let us hold two things together. First, this reflects a specific, terrible moment of covenant judgment in Israel's history — not a threat over believers today. Second, and more importantly, it shows us the depth of the ruin from which Christ came to save.

For into this kind of darkness, Jesus came. He entered a world under the shadow of sin and death, and He bore the full weight of judgment Himself, so that we might be spared. Where sin leads to unspeakable horror, Christ leads to life. However dark the passage, the cross is darker still — and there our rescue was won.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. Do I take the destructive power of sin seriously enough?
2. How does the depth of this darkness magnify the greatness of Christ's rescue?
3. Am I resting in the Saviour who entered our darkness to bring us out?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Lord, these words are hard to read, yet they show me how deep our ruin goes and how great Your rescue is. Thank You that Christ entered the darkness to bring me into light. Amen.
